title: Stay
full_review:
You may scratch your head about the dizzying plot turns in "Stay" (20th Century Fox), but chances are you won't be bored.

Director Marc Forster's follow-up to his gentle and stately J.M. Barrie biography, "Finding Neverland," could not be more different.

His latest is a cinematically dazzling mood piece involving psychiatrist Sam Foster (Ewan McGregor), who is called in to help a guilt-racked suicidal youth, Henry Letham (Ryan Gosling), who blames himself for his role in a deadly car accident that killed his parents, after the young man's own therapist takes a leave of absence.

The boy, as played with mesmerizing intensity by Gosling, projects scary menace, and at first you think he may turn into a dangerous stalker, as he disconcertingly shadows Sam at various locations. But it soon becomes clear that he genuinely needs help, believing he is going to hell for having "killed" his parents.

A random comment about an impending hailstorm -- not on the official weather report -- leads Sam to ponder Henry's prescient powers, but soon Sam is entrenched in a maze of deja-vu incidents, which is to say that the exact same scenes keep repeating over and over. He also encounters people from Henry's life -- like his mother (Kate Burton), who is mysteriously dripping blood, and her unfriendly dog -- who were purportedly dead.

Sam's girlfriend, Lila (Naomi Watts), was a former patient, and she has latent emotional problems of her own, but she worries about Sam, who (understandably) gives every sign of losing his mind.

The film's events are intentionally perplexing, so you may often need to sift mentally through the implications of what you've just seen. The screenplay is by David Benioff, author of the novel "The 25th Hour" (later filmed) and the script for "Troy."

Forster maintains a taut, creepy fever-dream atmosphere throughout, though the suspense level drops somewhat when the film reveals itself as more of a stylish exploration of truth and reality, and one involving fantastical elements at that, than a traditional mystery.

All the performances are excellent. The Scottish McGregor again plays with a convincing American accent and his rising paranoia in light of the strange events he witnesses are well delineated, while Watts makes a sympathetic sounding board for Sam's ravings. Burton, Bob Hoskins as Sam's blind colleague, Leon, and Janeane Garofalo as the therapist on leave are equally first-rate. The rest of the cast is filled out with solid New York actors: B.D. Wong, Amy Sedaris and Mary Testa among them.

Speaking of the Big Apple, the city that never sleeps is photographed by Roberto Schaefer in marvelously inventive ways, giving full measure to production designer Kevin Thompson's symbol-laden landscape, so that even familiar sights have a new perspective, all of which suit the surreal story.

This film contains a car crash, scattered rough and crude language and profanity, a suicide theme, brief sexual innuendo including some gyrating in a strip club, horror effects involving blood and a dog attack. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
